answers.answer: Caching could avoid repeatedly doing the 80 ms database build for the frequently reused station-language pairs. A hit uses a 2 ms cache lookup instead, and weekly changes make a reusable copy plausible, subject to an acceptable staleness and update policy. Use a key such as station-guide:42:en, including both station ID and requested language; Spanish must have a different key. The application API checks the cache. On a hit it returns the stored guide without this database build, although the copy could be stale. On a miss the application reads/builds the guide from the authoritative database, stores that fetched result in the cache, and returns it. The cache does not fetch or fill itself. A miss still incurs the 80 ms database work plus the cache lookup and cache write; storing the extra copy consumes memory and creates another copy to manage. The lookup is added to reads, and fills add writes. Losing a cache entry must not lose the guide source.

evidence.quote: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.
Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write.
The API finds product:42 in the cache and returns its stored details.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. A had already fetched the old database value before B committed. B deleted the key, but deletion did not cancel or change the value held by paused A. A then recreated the cache entry with that old value, so C hits it before expiry. The team cannot claim that every read after B finishes sees the new hours: C is a counterexample. A simple way to avoid this stale cached copy for an endpoint requiring the latest committed hours is to bypass this cache and read the authoritative database for the request. Under the given commit prerequisite and exact sequence, that subsequent database read sees B's new hours. The lesson does not teach a concurrency protocol that would make cache invalidation guarantee freshness; none is required here.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. To avoid charging an old price at checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

answers.answer: In case A, the 12:03 request can use the original cached forecast: it has not expired, even though the source changed at 12:02, so that hit is stale. At 12:11 the original entry has expired at 12:10, so the request must fetch the source and can then fill a new copy. In case B, the original copy was removed at 12:04 to free memory, so the 12:05 request misses and must fetch the source despite the original ten-minute TTL not having elapsed. The TTL sets the lifetime before expiration for this stored entry. It neither promises the copy stays present for all ten minutes nor promises freshness after source changes, and it does not perform a background refresh at 12:10. A later miss does the loading. TTL also does not bound the age of the underlying data supplied at fill time. Removal to free memory is eviction; it responds to capacity, while expiration responds to the entry lifetime.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: One shared cache is the simpler fit for the goal of one deletion removing the map entry used by all four instances, given that a 2 ms network lookup is acceptable and there are no concurrent fills. Today each lookup occurs inside the handling API process. Only the writer instance deletes its own entry, so requests routed to any of the other three instances can keep hitting their old maps. Their copies need their own updates or removal. With a shared cache, all four API instances look up the same entry in a separate cache service over the network. Deleting that single entry means the next request from any instance misses and can reload from the database. The tradeoff includes network lookup time and operating another service. If one local cache is lost, only that instance loses its copy; the other three retain theirs. If the shared cache is unreachable, all four instances lose access to that shared map entry. Sharing alone does not guarantee freshness with respect to database changes; the deletion policy still matters.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.

answers.answer: When the popular key expires, many simultaneous requests can all miss and each read the same schedule from the database. That repeats work and risks sending far more than its safe 500 reads per second. Coalesce the concurrent misses for the same schedule: let one request start the database lookup, have concurrent readers share that in-progress lookup and result, and fill the cache with the fetched schedule. This turns many duplicate reads into one lookup for that group. An entire cache outage lasts beyond a single refill and can redirect nearly all 10,000 requests per second to a database that supports only 500. During the outage, cap total fallback schedule reads across the API instances at what the database can safely handle, at most 500 per second here, and return temporary errors to excess requests instead of issuing database reads. This reduces database work by rejecting work beyond the safe budget. If a last known schedule remains available independently of the unreachable cache and is within the allowed 60 seconds, serve it to permitted requests without database work; do not rely on reading that schedule from the unavailable service. After the permitted age or without an accessible copy, use bounded fallback or temporary errors. The lesson teaches coalescing and bounded fallback but does not specify how to implement cross-instance coordination or where to retain an outage-accessible old copy.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

answers.answer: Do not add the proposed cache now. Each unique result is read exactly once, and the cache would be filled only after that read, so there is no later request to benefit from the stored result. The existing 2 ms database read is comfortably within the 100 ms budget, and ten reads per second are comfortably below the database's 1,000-read capacity. The proposal preserves every database read while adding cache writes, memory for unused copies, and management of those copies. If the application checks the cache on each request, those checks also add work while yielding misses for these unique results. Reconsider if results begin receiving repeated reads, especially if a small set becomes popular enough that reuse could materially reduce database load or response time. Measure those benefits and misses against the costs and freshness needs then.

evidence.quote: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.
Before a copy exists, the API still does the database lookup. Storing that copy uses memory and adds a cache write.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.
